title: Mitochondria Structure
content:
# Mitochondria Structure

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Describe the structure of mitochondria
- Explain how mitochondrial structure relates to function
- Understand where different stages of respiration occur
- Explain why some cells have more mitochondria than others

## Introduction

Mitochondria are the organelles where most aerobic respiration takes place. Their structure is highly specialised for ATP production. Understanding mitochondrial structure helps explain how cells efficiently produce energy.

## Key Concepts

### Overview of Mitochondria

**Key facts:**
- Found in nearly all eukaryotic cells
- Site of aerobic respiration
- Called the "powerhouse of the cell"
- Typically 1-10 μm long
- Number varies with cell energy needs

### Mitochondrial Structure

**Main features:**

| Structure | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| Outer membrane | Smooth, permeable to small molecules |
| Inner membrane | Highly folded, less permeable |
| Cristae | Folds of inner membrane |
| Matrix | Fluid-filled interior |
| Intermembrane space | Gap between membranes |

[DIAGRAM: Cross-section of mitochondrion showing all structures]

### The Outer Membrane

**Features:**
- Smooth and continuous
- Contains porins (protein channels)
- Permeable to small molecules and ions
- Separates mitochondria from cytoplasm

**Function:**
- Boundary of organelle
- Controls what enters/exits
- Relatively non-selective

### The Inner Membrane

**Features:**
- Highly folded into cristae
- Much less permeable than outer membrane
- Contains many proteins
- Contains electron transport chain
- Contains ATP synthase

**Function:**
- Site of oxidative phosphorylation
- Creates proton gradient
- Site of most ATP production

### Cristae

**What are they?**
- Folds of the inner membrane
- Project into the matrix
- Greatly increase surface area

**Why important?**
- More surface area for electron transport chain
- More ATP synthase enzymes
- More ATP can be produced

**Comparison:**
| Surface | Relative area |
|---------|---------------|
| Smooth inner membrane | 1x |
| Folded (cristae) | 5x or more |

### The Matrix

**Contains:**
- Enzymes for Krebs cycle
- Mitochondrial DNA
- Ribosomes (70S, like bacteria)
- Substrates and intermediates

**Functions:**
- Site of Krebs cycle
- Contains genetic material
- Produces some mitochondrial proteins

### Intermembrane Space

**Location:** Between outer and inner membranes

**Function:**
- Accumulates H⁺ ions (protons)
- Creates proton gradient
- Essential for ATP synthesis

### Structure-Function Relationships

| Structure | Adaptation | Function |
|-----------|------------|----------|
| Cristae | Large surface area | More ATP synthase and electron carriers |
| Matrix enzymes | High concentration | Efficient Krebs cycle |
| Inner membrane | Many proteins | Electron transport chain |
| Double membrane | Two compartments | Proton gradient possible |
| Own DNA | Semi-autonomous | Makes some proteins locally |

### Where Respiration Stages Occur

| Stage | Location | Products |
|-------|----------|----------|
| Glycolysis | Cytoplasm | 2 ATP, 2 pyruvate |
| Link reaction | Matrix | Acetyl CoA |
| Krebs cycle | Matrix | CO₂, reduced coenzymes |
| Oxidative phosphorylation | Inner membrane | Most ATP (~34) |

[DIAGRAM: Locations of respiration stages in mitochondrion]

### Mitochondrial DNA

**Key points:**
- Small, circular DNA molecule
- Encodes some mitochondrial proteins
- Inherited maternally (from egg cell only)
- Evidence for endosymbiotic theory

**Endosymbiotic theory:**
- Mitochondria evolved from bacteria
- Were engulfed by ancestral cells
- Became permanent organelles
- Retained own DNA and ribosomes

### Why Different Numbers of Mitochondria?

| Cell type | Mitochondria number | Reason |
|-----------|---------------------|--------|
| Muscle cells | Very many (thousands) | High energy for contraction |
| Liver cells | Many (~2000) | High metabolic activity |
| Red blood cells | None | No nucleus, no mitochondria |
| Fat cells | Few | Low metabolic rate |
| Sperm cells | Many (in midpiece) | Energy for swimming |

### Mitochondria in Active Cells

**Example: Muscle cell**
- Contains thousands of mitochondria
- Located near myofibrils (contractile units)
- Provides ATP for contraction
- Trained athletes have more mitochondria

**Example: Sperm cell**
- Mitochondria in midpiece
- Surrounds base of flagellum
- Powers tail movement
- Enables swimming to egg

[DIAGRAM: Sperm cell showing mitochondria location]

### Mitochondrial Health

**Mitochondrial diseases:**
- Caused by mutations in mitochondrial DNA
- Inherited maternally
- Affect high-energy demand organs
- Examples: muscle weakness, neurological problems

**Factors affecting mitochondria:**
| Factor | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| Exercise | Increases number and efficiency |
| Ageing | Decline in function |
| Toxins | Can damage mitochondria |
| Good nutrition | Supports function |

## Common Exam Questions

- Describe the structure of a mitochondrion
- Explain how cristae are adapted for ATP production
- State where the Krebs cycle occurs
- Explain why muscle cells have many mitochondria

## Common Misconceptions

- **Misconception:** All respiration happens in mitochondria
- **Reality:** Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm

- **Misconception:** Mitochondria produce energy
- **Reality:** Mitochondria transfer energy to ATP; energy comes from glucose

- **Misconception:** All cells have the same number of mitochondria
- **Reality:** Number varies with energy needs of the cell

- **Misconception:** Mitochondria have no genetic material
- **Reality:** They have their own circular DNA and ribosomes

## Practice Questions

1. Name the folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane. (1 mark)

2. State where in the mitochondrion the Krebs cycle occurs. (1 mark)

3. Explain how the structure of cristae is related to their function. (3 marks)

4. Suggest why muscle cells contain more mitochondria than skin cells. (2 marks)

5. Explain how the presence of DNA in mitochondria supports the endosymbiotic theory. (3 marks)

6. Describe the structure of a mitochondrion and explain how each part is adapted for its role in respiration. (6 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Mitochondrion | Organelle where aerobic respiration occurs |
| Cristae | Folds of inner mitochondrial membrane |
| Matrix | Fluid-filled interior of mitochondrion |
| Outer membrane | Smooth outer boundary of mitochondrion |
| Inner membrane | Folded membrane containing electron transport chain |
| Intermembrane space | Gap between outer and inner membranes |
| Endosymbiotic theory | Theory that mitochondria evolved from bacteria |

## Summary

- Mitochondria are the main site of aerobic respiration
- Structure: outer membrane, inner membrane (cristae), matrix, intermembrane space
- Cristae increase surface area for electron transport chain and ATP synthase
- Matrix contains Krebs cycle enzymes
- Inner membrane is site of oxidative phosphorylation
- Mitochondria have own DNA and ribosomes (endosymbiotic origin)
- Cells with high energy needs have more mitochondria
- Structure is highly adapted for efficient ATP production
